channelEconomics.topic: YouTube policy risk for faceless AI channels
channelEconomics.finding: YouTube requires original and authentic content and calls out AI content made with generic or unoriginal templates that gives an impression of mass production, templated repeat scenarios, and slideshow-style content with minimal narrative. Series remain eligible when each video is materially varied. AI personas posing as experts on health, legal, financial or political topics cannot monetise.

At documented prices a finished minute is roughly $1-15 in SaaS and about $3 hybrid (estimates above), so tool cost per video is small next to the originality and variation the platform policy demands. Cheaper generation raises the volume of near-identical output, which is exactly what the inauthentic-content policy targets.

FLUX.1 dev ships under a non-commercial licence (check output terms before monetised channels); Qwen-Image is Apache 2.0; Whisper MIT; HyperFrames Apache 2.0; FFmpeg LGPL (GPL if GPL components enabled) with a patent caution for commercial MPEG use; Remotion is free only up to 3 people.

checklist: Decide per video whether it shows a realistic person, place or event that did not happen, or a real person saying or doing something they did not. If yes, switch on the platform AI label on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, and add an on-screen or caption line as well.
Do not rely on auto-detection: platforms read C2PA metadata, but creators are still the ones required to disclose, and YouTube can suspend YPP for repeated non-disclosure.
Keep every AI character plainly an AI character. Never present one as a real person, a doctor, financial adviser or lawyer; YouTube's monetization page names an AI doctor as an example.

Do not publish batches of near-identical template videos. YouTube treats 'repetitive or mass-produced' content as ineligible for monetization; add original script, voice, editing or commentary to each.
Get written consent before cloning a real person's face or voice (GDPR: it relates to an identifiable person; biometric identification triggers Art. 9). Keep the consent on file.

If you build the avatar or generator tool yourself, check provider duties: machine-readable marking (Art. 50(2)) and telling users they are talking to an AI (Art. 50(1)). Existing systems have until 2 Dec 2026 for marking; new ones from 2 Aug 2026.
If you only publish with third-party tools, you are a deployer: disclose realistic deep fakes under Art. 50(4) since 2 Aug 2026, clearly and no later than first exposure.
Use only licensed music. On TikTok you confirm you hold all licences; check each platform's commercial music library before using tracks in brand or sales content.
Tick paid-promotion or branded-content tools on every sponsored or affiliate post and say so in the content itself (UCPD Annex I point 11; Reclamecode wording such as #ad or #advertentie).
Do not rely on owning copyright in output made with prompts alone. Add human-authored script, edits or arrangement and keep drafts as evidence.
Do not target or depict minors with AI characters until the platform's minor rules are read; DSA Art. 28 pushes platforms to enforce these.
Re-read the live platform policy page on the day you publish; three of the platform policy pages here could not be read this session.

gdprAndLiability.finding: The businesses decide purposes and means, so they are controllers. A founder who builds and runs agents on their data acts on their behalf and is a processor in most framings; if he decides purposes himself he risks controller status. EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 (final, adopted 7 July 2021) are the reference; only the landing page was read, so criteria are not quoted here. Two separate businesses (family and larger sibling) are separate controllers unless they jointly determine purposes; joint controllership was not researched (gap). Legal advice from a Dutch privacy lawyer is advisable.

Article 28 requires a binding contract: processing only on documented instructions, no sub-processor without controller authorisation, Art. 32 security measures, confidentiality of personnel, deletion or return of data at the end, and audit support. The text was read from a secondary reproduction. The Dutch AP page on the verwerkersovereenkomst returned 403 and its English variant returned 403; gap for AP-specific wording.

gdprAndLiability.topic: LLM provider as sub-processor: retention and training
gdprAndLiability.finding: Anthropic API: inputs and outputs deleted within 30 days by default, with exceptions (zero-retention agreement, longer-lived Files API, policy violations); commercial data is not used for training by default. OpenAI API: abuse-monitoring logs up to 30 days, zero data retention available on listed endpoints, no training on API data unless opted in. Gemini API: paid services are not used to improve products and fall under a Data Processing Addendum, unpaid services are used and may be human-reviewed, so only paid tiers fit business data. Treat the provider as a sub-processor that must be listed to the controllers.

OpenAI offers an EEA and Switzerland region (eu.api.openai.com) that requires approval for abuse monitoring controls and a Modified Retention amendment. Anthropic and Google EU residency terms were not researched (gap). Self-hosting the ERP keeps business data on the owners' hardware, but any prompt sent to a hosted LLM carries data out unless residency is contracted.

ERP-side: Frappe logs token requests against the token user; Odoo respects access rights and record rules in standard MCP mode. OWASP recommends logging, monitoring and rate limiting as secondary controls. Retention period for agent logs is a decision to document; no Dutch rule on this was verified.

OWASP LLM06: minimise tools, avoid open-ended tools, grant minimal downstream permissions, run in the user's security context, enforce authorisation in downstream systems. Odoo: PostgreSQL user must not be a superuser.

Odoo documentation: daily backups of databases and filestore, copied to a remote archive server not accessible from the host. Backups of personal data fall under the same retention and deletion duties; deletion-on-request across backups was not researched (gap). Frappe docker docs read give no backup numbers.

metricsToWatch.metric: Free RAM, lower tail (windows_memory_available_bytes, p5 over a window)
metricsToWatch.why: Agent fleets spike memory; the low tail shows how close a box gets to stalling. USE method treats any saturation as a potential problem.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: No source gives a numeric threshold. Practice: alert on available-memory p5 falling below a floor Frank sets from observed baseline. Frank's own 4 GiB Windows safety floor is local policy, not from these sources.

metricsToWatch.metric: Swap, commit and compression pressure (windows_memory_committed_bytes vs commit_limit; modified page list; page faults; Linux /proc/pressure/memory)
metricsToWatch.why: Memory saturation shows up as paging or stalls before OOM. PSI 'full' means all non-idle tasks stalled at once, described as a thrashing state.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Sources define the signals but give no recommended alert thresholds (the PSI page's 150 ms/1 s and 50 ms/1 s values are API examples, not guidance). Practice: alert on sustained committed/limit ratio near 1 or sustained PSI full > 0.

metricsToWatch.why: USE method: 100% typically a bottleneck; for non-interruptible resources like disks, sustained use above 70% warrants investigation. Google chose CPU consumption over QPS as the capacity measure.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Documented: investigate sustained >70% on disk-like resources; 100% = bottleneck (USE page). Not a CPU-specific paging rule.

metricsToWatch.metric: Queue depth / saturation (job queue length, litellm_in_flight_requests, executor load)
metricsToWatch.why: Saturation is the golden signal for how full the service is; queued work that cannot be serviced is a USE saturation measure. Google favours rejecting excess load over unbounded queues.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: USE page: any non-zero saturation is a potential problem. No numeric queue limit documented for agent fleets; set from baseline (practice).

metricsToWatch.metric: Token spend per task and daily spend (LiteLLM response_cost, spend metrics, Langfuse cost)
metricsToWatch.why: Cloud API cost is the only variable cost that scales with agent count.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Documented mechanism: max_budget with budget_duration per key/user/team, plus soft-budget alerts and remaining-budget metrics. Dollar amounts are Frank's to set; no source gives one.

metricsToWatch.metric: Completion time per task, as percentiles (gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration, gen_ai.client.operation.duration)
metricsToWatch.why: SRE book warns averages hide tails: 100 ms average at 1,000 rps can still mean 1% of requests take 5 s. Use histograms.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Alert on p95/p99 against a baseline Frank sets; no numeric target in sources. LiteLLM alerting_threshold is configured in seconds for slow/hanging calls (example value 300 in the doc).

metricsToWatch.why: Retry storms amplify overload. Google guidance: max 3 retries per request, and retry only when retries are under 10% of requests.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Documented limits above are design rules; alert when retry ratio exceeds 10% (derived from the per-client rule, practice for alerting). Failed-call and hanging-call alerts exist in LiteLLM.

metricsToWatch.metric: Error rate (failed LLM calls, failed jobs)
metricsToWatch.why: Errors are a golden signal and USE dimension; Prometheus guidance says page on user-visible errors high in the stack.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Alert on symptoms; for batch jobs wait at least 2 full job cycles before paging (Prometheus practice doc).

metricsToWatch.metric: GPU memory used and GPU utilization (nvidia-smi --query-gpu, DCGM exporter, nvidia_gpu_exporter)
metricsToWatch.why: VRAM exhaustion kills local-model jobs; utilization shows idle paid capacity.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: No source gives a threshold. Practice: alert on VRAM used / total near full for a sustained window.

metricsToWatch.why: Always-on mini PCs and GPU nodes throttle when hot; temperature is exposed by nvidia-smi, DCGM, Beszel.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: No source gives a safe temperature. Use the GPU vendor's published limit for the exact card (not fetched).

metricsToWatch.metric: Node and job liveness (push heartbeat from each scheduled job; HTTP/TCP checks)
metricsToWatch.why: Detects silent failure of always-on boxes and cron-style agents. Uptime Kuma push monitors let a job report in.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Alert when heartbeat missing; interval floor 20 s per Uptime Kuma. Interval to match job cadence (practice).

metricsToWatch.metric: Disk free and growth (windows logical_disk, Langfuse ClickHouse/S3 growth)
metricsToWatch.why: Langfuse docs say observability data is large; storage is the first thing that fills on a small box.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Use predict_linear to alert on projected fill time; the horizon is a choice (practice).

metricsToWatch.metric: Monitoring-of-monitoring (is the alert pipeline itself working)
metricsToWatch.why: Prometheus docs recommend a blackbox test that alerts flow end to end.
metricsToWatch.alertRule: Send a periodic always-firing test alert to the notification channel and alarm on its absence.

capacityPlanning.finding: For every resource check utilization, saturation and errors. 100% utilization is typically a bottleneck; sustained >70% on disk-like non-interruptible resources deserves investigation; any non-zero saturation is a potential problem. Applies to software resources such as thread pools too.
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation; 'if you can only measure four metrics', use these. Saturation emphasises the most constrained resource.
Measure distributions, not means; bucket request counts by latency. Averages hide a slow tail (1% at 5 s behind a 100 ms mean).

capacityPlanning.method: Measure capacity in resource terms, not request counts
capacityPlanning.finding: Google models capacity as CPU consumption rather than QPS because per-request cost varies by type, time and client. For agent fleets this argues for sizing in tokens, RAM and VRAM per task type rather than 'tasks per hour'. The translation to agents is practice, not stated by the source.

capacityPlanning.method: Shed load rather than queue unboundedly
capacityPlanning.finding: Accept only what can be processed; unbounded queueing causes memory exhaustion and cascades. Retry limits: max 3 per request, retry only if under 10% of requests are retries.

Specify requirements (reliability target, redundancy such as N+2) rather than concrete allocations; spreadsheet plans go stale and are brittle to small changes. The source gives no headroom percentage.

capacityPlanning.method: Match reliability and provisioning to need
capacityPlanning.finding: Over-provisioning for maximum reliability has direct and opportunity costs; the book cites throughput-optimized clusters running hot at 10-50% of the cost of low-latency clusters (a Bigtable example, not a general rule).
Prometheus practice doc lists capacity as an alert category because it needs intervention before outages; batch/offline work should look at throughput and job success over at least 2 cycles.
predict_linear(v, t) extrapolates a gauge t seconds ahead via simple linear regression; good for disk and storage fill, weak for bursty demand.
PSI 'some' vs 'full' quantifies time lost to memory, CPU or IO contention in 10/60/300 s windows via /proc/pressure/memory. Linux only; kernel doc gives no alert thresholds.

llmCostTracking.finding: Virtual keys carry max_budget (USD) and budget_duration (e.g. 30s, 30m, 24h, 30d) per key, user, team or end-user; also TPM, RPM and max-parallel limits. Requires a Postgres database, otherwise budget checks are skipped. Budget reservation is on by default so concurrent requests cannot overshoot. Models priced at zero (self-hosted) are excluded from budget checks.

All calls land in LiteLLM_SpendLogs with key hash, user, team, tags, model, prompt/completion/total tokens and USD spend; response cost is also in the x-litellm-response-cost header. Payload includes status, latency (time to first token if streaming), cost breakdown, cache costs. Retention policy not documented in pages fetched.

/metrics exposes spend per user/key/team, tokens, remaining budget, failed/total requests, latency histograms, litellm_in_flight_requests. Requires prometheus callback in config; /metrics needs a LiteLLM API key by default in recent versions (doc says since v1.85.0).
Soft budget alerts and periodic reports plus failure and hanging-call alerts to Slack, Discord, Teams or webhook; digest mode reduces repeats.

Cost attaches to each generation. Ingested provider cost wins over inferred cost; inference uses model definitions (regex match plus per-token-type prices); custom models can be added for fine-tuned or self-hosted models. Per task cost needs traces grouped by session or trace id.

Langfuse accepts OTLP over HTTP (JSON or protobuf, not gRPC) at /api/public/otel with Basic auth; header x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4 avoids up-to-10-minute delay. Langfuse prefers langfuse.* attributes over generic OTel ones. GenAI duration and agent metrics are named in OTel conventions but still in Development.

llmCostTracking.approach: Cost of running the tracker itself
llmCostTracking.finding: Langfuse self-hosting pulls in ClickHouse, Postgres, Redis and S3 with a 16 GiB RAM, 100 GiB recommended VM; on a disk-constrained box that overhead may exceed the API spend it tracks. LiteLLM alone needs only Postgres. Whether to choose Langfuse Cloud instead was not evaluated (pricing not fetched).
